slide_title: Gas Exchange Surfaces: Insect Tracheal Systems
original_text: Gas Exchange Surfaces Insects Insects have inefficient circulation nHemolymph fluid just contained within the hemocoel cavity Insects overcome inefficiency with system of tubes called tracheantrachea  tubules  tracheoles  ~0.1um tubes nMeans nearly every cell is near an air tube Deliver air directly to the cells without entering the blood Air sacs act like bellows to move air into and out from the trachea tubes
explanation: Insects have an open circulatory system, where hemolymph is contained within the open hemocoel cavity, making it inefficient for gas transport. To overcome this, insects utilize a tracheal system consisting of a network of air tubes (tracheae) that branch into smaller tubules and finally microscopic tracheoles (~0.1 $\mu m$). This network ensures that nearly every cell is near an air tube, delivering oxygen directly to tissues without utilizing blood. Air sacs act as bellows, inflating and deflating to pump air through the tracheal tubes.

questions.q: How do insects overcome the inefficiency of their open circulatory system for gas exchange?
opts: They have highly vascularized internal lungs.
They utilize a countercurrent exchange system in their skin.
They use a system of branching tracheal tubes that deliver air directly to cells without using blood.
They rely on active transport of oxygen through the hemolymph.
questions.exp: Insects use a tracheal system (trachea, tubules, tracheoles) to deliver air directly to cells, bypassing the circulatory system entirely.

questions.q: What is the function of air sacs in the insect respiratory system?
opts: To act like bellows to move air into and out of the tracheal tubes
To perform countercurrent exchange with hemolymph
questions.exp: Air sacs in insects act as bellows, inflating and deflating to draw air in and push it through the tracheal network.
